newsitem.title: USA: Ehrlich sees Q4 US GDP boost from trade data--RFTV.
newsitem.headline: Ehrlich sees Q4 US GDP boost from trade data--RFTV.

text.p: A senior Commerce Department on Friday said the latest figures on international trade suggest net exports will be a positive contributor to gross domestic product growth for the fourth quarter of this year.
"It's going to have a significant positive effect on fourth quarter GDP," U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich told Reuters Financial Television.

"In the last several days, I think we've had to rewrite our view of the U.S. economy in the fourth quarter based on these data today and the data on retail trade that we received earlier in the week," he added.

Earlier on Friday, the Commerce Department reported that the U.S. trade deficit widened by 4.9 percent to $8.4 billion in November. Despite the widening, the gap was far smaller than the monthly deficits in the double digits recorded earlier this year.
U.S. GDP advanced by 2.1 percent in the third quarter of this year. The Commerce Department is scheduled to provide its advance estimate of fourth quarter growth on January 31.
"The economy in the fourth quarter seemed to have quite a head of steam and is entering 1997 with far more momentum than we thought," Ehrlich said.

Commenting on potential risks stemming from the fact that economy is running at rather high levels of capacity, Ehrlich said, "We're certainly operating at fairly robust levels of capacity utilization and fairly low levels of unemployment."
However, he pointed out that the economy has been operating close to those levels for some time and done so without an "explosion" in final prices.
The Federal Reserve said Friday that U.S. industrial capacity utilization rose in December to 83.8 percent from 83.4 percent in November. The U.S. unemployment rate now stands at 5.3 percent.
Regarding the capacity utilization rate, Ehrlich said, "I think that the issue is more a caution than it is an alarm bell and it's true for the unemployment rate as well."
Asked about the deficit with China, which worsened earlier this year but improved in November, Ehrlich emphasized that the long-term issue revolves around exports not imports.
"The problem is not our imports from China. The problem is the absence of our exports to China," he said, pointing out that U.S. exports to China have been flat despite growth in that economy.
